text:
jamie_support: FYI incoming from a customer (mentioned @sara) - they upgraded billing yesterday and now see intermittent 429s. They say only one API key in use but requests come from a pool of NATed IPs. Can we confirm which quota wins: org vs project vs key vs IP?
lee_oncall: Thanks Jamie. Can you paste a couple of request IDs and the exact response body for the 429s? Also sample request headers (no API secret).
jamie_support: Pasted from customer logs (redacted):
```
status: 429
body: {"error":"rate_limit_exceeded","message":"Rate limit exceeded","scopes":["org:proj","ip:203.0.113.5"]}
headers:
  x-request-id: rq_3b7e2f
  x-rate-limit-reset: 171000
  Authorization: Bearer sk-live-REDACTED
  X-Forwarded-For: 203.0.113.5, 198.51.100.7
```
jamie_support: They also included a curl repro they run from their load balancer: `curl -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-live-REDACTED" https://api.redwood.example/v1/generate -d '{"prompt":"hi"}'`
miguel_infra: Quick note: with NAT/load-balancers we often see many backend IPs but only one public egress. If their load balancer preserves client IPs in X-Forwarded-For we might be using that for IP-based limits. Do we currently prefer IP-derived scope over API key when both present? :thinking:
lee_oncall: Current behavior: precedence is API key > project > org > IP for quota attribution in the common path, BUT if the request lacks a valid key or if the key maps to a different org/project than the one in the token metadata we fallback to IP-derived heuristics. That fallback can cause surprising attribution when proxies mutate headers.
kate_billing: I checked billing for their org (acme-search). They did move to a higher commit but the org-level committed capa is different than project-level. If org commit is exhausted, we will see org-level 429s even if project has a small allowance left.
jamie_support: The customer's 429 body specifically listed both scopes which made them confused: `scopes:["org:proj","ip:203.0.113.5"]`. They asked why the API key didn't take precedence.
miguel_infra: Two common edge cases: 1) their Authorization token might be rotated and the header sent is one we don't recognize (we then try to attribute by IP). 2) Their proxy may strip or rewrite the Authorization header before hitting our edge (happens with some WAFs). Can they confirm the token value on their side matches exactly?
lee_oncall: For repro steps I recommend: (1) curl with valid key from one NAT IP -> observe quota attributed to API key; (2) curl with same payload but intentionally remove Authorization header -> should attribute to IP/org; (3) simulate header rewrite by sending Authorization that resolves to different org -> observe fallback behavior. Patch suggestion: add 'x-client-auth-origin' header (internal only) for proxied clients so we don't fallback to IP.
jamie_support: I asked customer to run the three steps and to provide x-request-id from failing requests. Also suggested rotating the key as a quick workaround and to test from a single egress IP.
kate_billing: If rotation/egress consolidation doesn't help we can temporarily raise org-level burst allowance for their billing account while they migrate. I'll need the org id and a support ticket to authorize.
prod_telemetry_bot: Alert summary: 429 spike detected for org: org_acme (rate +420% over baseline). Top IPs: 203.0.113.5, 203.0.113.6. Top failing token: sk-live-REDACTED (last seen: 1732001060).
lee_oncall: Thanks — once we have the x-request-ids we can trace the exact attribution path in logs (auth lookup -> project mapping -> quota evaluation). I'll also drop a short diag query to show whether the failing requests hit our auth cache and what looked up org/project was.
jamie_support: Perfect. I'll follow up with the customer steps and escalate if the logs show header stripping. Closing this thread when we have the x-request-ids. :white_check_mark:
